headline: Federal charges widen legal fight over Williston ICE facility protests
dek: Five people are accused of repeatedly blocking access to the Vermont facility, while separate state trespass cases are moving forward against protesters arrested this summer.
body: Federal prosecutors have charged five people accused of repeatedly blocking access to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Williston, opening a new legal track in a protest campaign that has already produced separate state trespass cases.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Vermont said Sept. 30 that Peter Booth, 58, of Jericho; Lexington Kennedy, 22, of New York City; Henry Prensky, 80, of Burlington; Roan Wade, 23, of Red Hook, New York; and Sherri Wormser, 57, of Colchester were charged by information with obstructing access to the ICE National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center. The facility is in the White Cap business park in Williston, according to the [Department of Justice announcement](https://www.justice.gov/usao-vt/pr/five-people-charged-obstructing-access-federal-facility-williston-vermont).

The allegations involve three protest dates. Prosecutors say all five entered the building’s atrium on Feb. 9 and used their bodies to block doors leading to the federal facility after warnings to disperse. The Justice Department says Booth and Prensky did so again on May 14, while Kennedy and Wade repeated the conduct on July 24. In each instance, the release says, access was restored after law enforcement removed protesters from the building.

The federal case is narrower than a general challenge to protest activity: the charging document alleges obstruction of entrances and exits, not simply opposition to immigration policy. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Ophardt said the blockades created safety risks for people working at the facility and required a substantial police response. Those are the government’s allegations, not findings by a court.

The defendants have not yet been scheduled for initial appearances. The Justice Department said each faces up to 30 days in prison and a fine of up to $5,000 if convicted, with any sentence to be set by the court under the applicable factors. The agency also said the five had not retained or been appointed counsel when the announcement was issued. All five are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty.

The charges add to a separate Vermont prosecution arising from a July 24 demonstration at the same office complex. Vermont Attorney General Charity Clark filed unlawful-trespass cases against 13 people arrested during that sit-in; twelve pleaded not guilty at a Sept. 24 arraignment, and the case of an 18-year-old was transferred to family court. [Vermont Public’s reporting](https://www.vermontpublic.org/local-news/2026-09-24/vermont-attorney-general-charges-protesters-for-trespassing-at-ice-surveillance-facility) said the state charge carries a maximum of three months in prison, a $500 fine, or both.

Vermont Public reported Oct. 1 that three of the five people named in the federal case also face state charges. The outlet described the federal action as an escalation after Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George previously declined to prosecute some protesters arrested during sit-ins, while Clark’s office later took up the July cases. That split has made charging decisions part of the local debate over how Vermont should respond to civil disobedience at the facility.

For Williston, the immediate issue is practical as well as legal. The White Cap complex has become a recurring site of demonstrations, arrests and competing claims about public safety, federal immigration enforcement and protest rights. The next concrete step in the federal matter is the defendants’ initial court appearance; until then, the charging information establishes what prosecutors allege but does not resolve whether the conduct violated federal law or how the cases will affect future demonstrations.
author: NorthEast News Desk
